subject: anaesthesia
title: Perioperative cardiopulmonary resuscitation: theatre arrest to ROSC

steps.tx: Early recognition of theatre arrest starts with **standard monitors**. Watch the ECG, capnography waveform, blood pressure trend and alarms continuously during every case. Learn the common rhythms behind collapse, including ventricular fibrillation, severe bradycardia and anaphylaxis. Place the patient supine, remove the drapes, stop volatiles and insufflation, call for help and bring the arrest trolley. Regular **arrest drills** with checked defibrillators, labelled drugs and clear team roles save minutes, and **early recognition** by the whole team matters most.
steps.say: Recognising arrest early in theatre is the skill examiners reward most. Keep your eyes on the ECG, the capnography trace, the pressure trend and every alarm through the case. Ventricular fibrillation, profound bradycardia and anaphylaxis cause most perioperative collapses. Lay the patient flat, take the drapes down, switch off volatiles and insufflation, call for help and fetch the arrest trolley. Rehearse these drills with your team so everyone knows their role when the alarm sounds.

steps.tx: **Effective compressions** continue over light drapes with full chest recoil and minimal pauses, while one member manages the airway on 100 percent oxygen. Apply **defibrillation pads** with gel early and shock shockable rhythms without delay. Give adrenaline for arrest and anaphylaxis, treat suxamethonium bradycardia with atropine or glycopyrrolate, and replace fluids and blood during bleeding. Assign a compressor, an airway lead and a scribe, and use **capnography** to judge compression quality and detect ROSC.
steps.say: Start compressions immediately, even over light drapes, and allow full recoil between pushes with the smallest possible pauses. One person should manage the airway and deliver 100 percent oxygen throughout. Place the defibrillation pads on the chest early while compressions are continuing, and deliver a shock for ventricular fibrillation promptly. Use adrenaline for cardiac arrest and anaphylaxis, reverse suxamethonium bradycardia with atropine, and transfuse fluids and blood for bleeding. Rotate the compressor before fatigue builds, record every time and dose, and watch capnography for quality and return of circulation.

steps.tx: This illustration shows an operating room team performing CPR on a draped patient. One clinician delivers **chest compressions** at the centre of the exposed chest while another holds the airway and gives oxygen. **Defibrillator pads** sit on the chest wall for rapid rhythm assessment and shock, and a monitor displays the **capnography trace** that judges compression quality. Note the assigned roles around the table, because clear compressors, airway leads and scribes save time in a real arrest.
steps.say: Look at this operating room scene and fix the roles in your memory. One person compresses the centre of the chest while another holds the airway and gives oxygen. The pads on the chest wall connect to the defibrillator for fast rhythm checks and shocks. The monitor shows the capnography waveform, which tells you whether compressions generate output and whether circulation has returned. Examiners love asking who does what around the table, so rehearse these positions with your team.

steps.tx: **Anaphylaxis** from chlorhexidine or latex presents with collapse and bronchospasm, and adrenaline remains the first treatment. **Local anaesthetic toxicity** after bupivacaine causes seizures and arrest, and lipid emulsion forms the specific rescue. Control **massive bleeding** with pressure, cell salvage, tranexamic acid and transfusion. Relieve tamponade and tension pneumothorax surgically, wash out venous air embolism, correct hypoxia, hypercarbia and electrolytes, rewarm the hypothermic patient, and consider femoral bypass or crash ECMO when circulation will not return.
steps.say: Always hunt for a reversible cause while compressions continue. Anaphylaxis from chlorhexidine or latex responds to adrenaline, while bupivacaine toxicity brings seizures and needs lipid emulsion. Bleeding demands pressure, cell salvage, tranexamic acid and transfusion. The surgeon relieves tamponade and tension pneumothorax, venous air embolism needs aspiration and source control, and you must correct hypoxia, electrolytes and hypothermia. When nothing restores output, femoral bypass or crash ECMO can bridge the patient.

steps.tx: **Post resuscitation care** begins the moment ROSC returns, with stabilisation, ICU handover and neuroprognostic follow up over days. Hold a **structured debrief** for the team, the patient and the family, and file an incident report so the whole service learns. Restock the trolley, check drugs and defibrillators, and review checklists before the next case. Avoid moving unstable patients too early, replace blame culture with learning, close **arrest documentation** gaps, and protect rest so fatigue never causes the next arrest.
steps.say: Care does not end when the pulse returns, because stabilisation, ICU handover and neurological follow up decide the final outcome. Debrief the team, speak honestly with the family, and file the incident report so the department keeps learning. Restock the trolley and check every drug and defibrillator before the next list. Never move an unstable patient too early, never let blame silence juniors, and write complete notes that protect both the patient and the team.
